title: The Stalk of Grass 3
content:
Lan Sizhui’s grip slipped reflexively. Before the oil lamp could shatter across the floorboards, Wei Wuxian caught it midair. With practiced calm, he brushed the wick against the burning fire talisman still pinched between the boy’s other fingers, set the glowing lamp on the table, and said breezily, "Did you craft all of these yourself, Granny? Beautiful handiwork."

Only then did the disciples realize that the silent crowd filling the hall wasn’t flesh and blood at all—they were paper mortuary figures.

Crafted life-sized, the figures were remarkably detailed. There were men, women, and young pages. The men were styled as underworld wardens, broad-shouldered and imposing, their features frozen in stylized fury. The women were modeled after noble maidens, their hair styled in delicate buns or tumbling loops; even beneath their billowy paper gowns, their forms curved gracefully, and the painted patterns on their robes looked richer than fine silk. Some were splashed with bright inks of garish red and jade green, while others remained stark white, bare paper waiting for brushwork. Bright, circular dabs of crimson rouge bloomed across every pair of chalk-white cheeks to fake the flush of life. But their pupils had been left blank—just stark white gaps where their eyes should have been. The brighter the red on their cheeks, the more chilling they looked in the dark.

Near the back of the hall stood another table holding several half-burned candles. Wei Wuxian lit them one by one, filling the room with a warm yellow glow. Aside from the paper figures, the hall was flanked by two enormous funerary wreaths, while the corners were heaped high with paper gold ingots, spirit money, and tiered funeral pagodas.

Jin Ling’s blade had already cleared its sheath by three fingers. Realizing this was just a shop selling funeral goods, he let out a quiet breath of relief and slid his sword home. When high-ranking cultivators passed away, the great clans never bothered with these eerie, theatrical superstitions common among ordinary mortals. Having seen very little of such customs, the boys quickly shook off their panic, their dread giving way to goosebump-prickled curiosity—honestly finding this creepier and far more thrilling than an ordinary beast hunt.

No matter how dense the fog outside was, it couldn't bleed through the wood, and for the first time since setting foot in Yi City, they could actually see each other's faces clearly. Feeling the tension ease, Wei Wuxian turned back to the old woman. "Could we trouble you for the use of your kitchen?"

The old crone seemed almost hostile toward the firelight, glaring balefully at the oil lamp. "Kitchen's out back. Use it yourselves." Without another word, she shuffled into an adjoining room like she was dodging the plague, slamming the door hard enough to make the boys flinch.

"That old hag is up to something," Jin Ling muttered. "You..."

"Alright, that's enough," Wei Wuxian cut in. "I need an extra pair of hands. Who's coming?"

Lan Sizhui stepped forward immediately. "I'll help."

Lan Jingyi remained standing straight as a pine. "What about me?"

"Stay put," Wei Wuxian said. "If I haven't told you to move, don't twitch."

Lan Sizhui followed Wei Wuxian into the kitchen out back. The moment they crossed the threshold, a wave of rancid mold and putrid rot hit them square in the face. Sizhui had never encountered a stench this foul in his entire life; his vision swam, but he bit the inside of his cheek and forced himself to stay. Jin Ling trailed behind them, but no sooner had he crossed the doorway than he jumped back out, fanning the air frantically with his sleeves. "What in the hell is that smell?! Aren't you supposed to be treating the poison? What are you doing in here?!"

Wei Wuxian looked back with an easy grin. "Oh, perfect timing! How did you know I was going to call you over? Come lend a hand."

"I'm not here to help you!" Jin Ling gagged. "Ugh! Did someone murder someone in here and forget to bury the body?!"

Wei Wuxian sighed. "Well, Young Mistress Jin, are you coming or what? If you're in, get your hands dirty. If not, go sit down and send someone else back."

Jin Ling flared up instantly. "Who are you calling Young Mistress?! Watch your mouth!" He pinched his nose, visibly wrestling with whether to bolt, before finally sneering, "Fine. I want to see what kind of nonsense you're pulling." Lifting the hems of his golden robes, he marched in, only for Wei Wuxian to yank open a wooden crate on the floor with a loud clatter.

The foul stench poured straight out of the box. Rotting inside was a pork hock and a whole chicken, their red flesh mottled with splotches of putrid green, crawling with tiny white maggots.

Jin Ling was driven right out the door again. Wei Wuxian hefted the crate and shoved it into his arms. "Take this out and toss it. Anywhere's fine, just far enough that we don't have to smell it."

Nauseated and deeply suspicious, Jin Ling did as he was told. He scrubbed his fingers aggressively with a silk handkerchief before hurling the fabric into the weeds. When he stormed back into the kitchen, he found Wei Wuxian and Lan Sizhui had hauled up two fresh buckets of well water from the courtyard and were already scrubbing down the room. "What are you two doing?" Jin Ling demanded.

Sizhui, scrubbing the grime from the counter with diligent elbow grease, replied, "As you can see, cleaning the stove."

"Why bother cleaning the stove? It's not like you're cooking."

"Who said we aren't?" Wei Wuxian countered naturally. "We're making food. Grab that feather duster over there and clear out all the cobwebs along the ceiling."

He said it with such casual authority that Jin Ling found himself holding the duster before he could even process what was happening, dusting the rafters in a daze. The more he swept, the more ridiculous it felt. Just as he was about to chuck the duster at Wei Wuxian's head, Wei Wuxian popped open a second crate, sending Jin Ling darting back again—though this time, no foul odor emerged.

Working in tandem, the three of them made quick work of the room. The kitchen was soon spotless, finally carrying a hint of human warmth rather than feeling like a derelict haunted house. Piling split firewood from the corner beneath the hearth, they sparked it with a fire talisman, set a washed iron cauldron over the flames, and brought a pot of water to a rolling boil. Wei Wuxian tipped a measure of glutinous rice from the second crate, washed it clean, and dropped it into the bubbling water.

Jin Ling frowned. "Congee?"

"Yep," Wei Wuxian replied.

Jin Ling hurled his rag to the ground.

Wei Wuxian tutted, "Look at that temper. You do five minutes of chores and blow a gasket. Look at Sizhui—worked the hardest out of anyone and hasn't complained once. What's wrong with congee?"

"What's good about it?! It's watery slop! Wait... I'm not mad about the congee!"

"Doesn't matter anyway," Wei Wuxian said breezily. "It's not for you."

Jin Ling blew his top. "What did you say?! I busted my back helping out, and I don't even get a bowl?!"

Lan Sizhui looked up from the hearth. "Young Master Mo, does congee neutralize corpse poisoning?"

Wei Wuxian chuckled. "It does, though it's not the congee that does the trick—it's the glutinous rice. An old folk remedy. Usually, you'd pack raw glutinous rice directly onto the bite or claw wound. If you ever run into this sort of mess in the future, remember that. It stings like hell, but it works like a charm. The effect is immediate. Since the boys didn't get scratched and only inhaled the powdered toxin, our only option is to brew up a pot of glutinous rice congee and have them drink it down."

Understanding dawned on Sizhui's face. "So that's why you insisted on coming inside, and why it had to be a house with people living in it. Only an inhabited home would have a kitchen, and only a kitchen would have glutinous rice."

"Who knows how long that rice has been sitting in a dark box, or if it's even edible?" Jin Ling pointed out. "Besides, this kitchen hasn't been touched in at least a year. It was caked in dust and the meat had turned completely rotten. Has that old crone not eaten a bite of food for an entire year? It's not like she's reached the inedia stage of cultivation—how has she survived?"

"Either this place has been abandoned the whole time and she isn't the owner," Wei Wuxian said, "or she simply doesn't need to eat."

Sizhui lowered his voice. "Not needing to eat means she's a corpse. But the old woman was clearly breathing."

Wei Wuxian casually stirred the pot, tossing in random spices and sauces from various jars along the shelf as he spoke. "By the way, you never finished telling me—how did you all end up in Yi City together? Don't tell me it was just a coincidence running into us here."

The atmosphere sobered instantly. Jin Ling spoke first: "Me, the Lan disciples, and a few others from the minor clans—we were all chasing the same thing. I tracked it all the way from Qinghe."

"We trailed it from Langya," Sizhui added.

"What were you chasing?" Wei Wuxian asked.

Sizhui shook his head. "We don't know. It never showed its face. We couldn't tell if it was an entity, a person... or some kind of organization."

A few days back, Jin Ling had tricked his uncle into a wild goose chase to help Wei Wuxian escape. Terrified that Jiang Cheng would actually carry out his threat to snap his legs, the boy had decided to vanish for ten days to a fortnight, planning to lay low until his uncle cooled off. He’d handed Zidian over to Jiang Cheng's trusted lieutenant and slipped away. He made it to a border town near Qinghe, looking for a promising night-hunt, and checked into a large inn for the night. While running through sword incantations in his room, Fairy had suddenly started barking at the door. It was well past midnight. Jin Ling hushed the spiritual hound, only to hear a soft knocking at the wood.

Fairy stopped barking, but grew restless, clawing frantic grooves into the floorboards with low growls rattling in his throat. Jin Ling called out to ask who was there, but received no reply, so he ignored it. Half an incense stick later, the knocking returned.

Jin Ling had slipped out the window with Fairy, looped around the street, and crept up from the ground floor to ambush the prankster from behind. But the corridor was dead empty. He waited in the shadows, but nobody approached his room.

Staying on guard, he left Fairy posted at the threshold, ready to pounce on anyone who came near, spending the entire night without a wink of sleep. Nothing else happened, save for an unsettling sound that dripped steadily through the dark like falling water.

The next morning, screaming tore through the hallway. Jin Ling kicked his door open, stepping straight into a thick pool of blood. Something plummeted from the doorframe above, and he leaped back just in time to dodge it.

A dead black cat.

Someone had secretly pinned the carcass directly over his lintel. The dripping he'd heard all night was the cat’s blood falling onto the floorboards.

"Every inn I stayed at after that was the exact same story," Jin Ling explained. "So I started actively hunting it down. Whenever I heard rumors of dead cats turning up out of nowhere, I went to investigate. I'm going to drag whoever is behind this into the light."

Wei Wuxian turned to Sizhui. "You experienced the same thing?"

Sizhui nodded. "Yes. A few days ago, we were night-hunting in Langya. During dinner one evening, our soup arrived with an unskinned cat's head floating in the broth... At first, we didn't realize we were being targeted, but when we switched inns that night, we found a slaughtered cat tucked inside our bedcovers. It kept happening for days. We followed the trail to Yueyang, crossed paths with Young Master Jin, and realized we were investigating the exact same thing, so we joined forces. We only reached this region today. Passing a village by a stone marker, we asked a local hunter for directions, and he pointed us straight down the road to Yi City."

A hunter? Wei Wuxian thought.

The disciples must have passed the village near the boundary marker well after he and Lan Wangji did. Yet they hadn't seen a single hunter—only a few bashful farm girls feeding chickens, who claimed the men of the village had gone off to haul freight and wouldn't be back for weeks.

The more Wei Wuxian pieced the threads together, the darker his expression grew.

From the sound of it, the culprit had done nothing beyond butchering cats and dumping the carcasses. Gruesome and terrifying as it seemed, the boys hadn't sustained a scratch; if anything, the grisly breadcrumbs had simply baited their youthful pride, daring them to chase the mystery to the bitter end.

On top of that, their paths had converged in Yueyang—the very same city from which Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji had journeyed south toward Eastern Shu. It looked less like a coincidence and more like someone had carefully orchestrated the board, herding these inexperienced juniors right into their path.

Luring a gaggle of greenhorn disciples to a lethal, unknown location to face the bloodthirsty remnants of a dismembered corpse—wasn't this the exact same script used back at Mo Village?

And that wasn't even the most concerning part. What truly kept Wei Wuxian on edge was the chilling possibility that the Yin Tiger Tally might very well be here in Yi City right now.

Much as he hated entertaining the thought, it was the only theory that fit. After all, someone had already managed to forge half a replica of the Tally; even if that rogue had supposedly been dealt with, who could say whose hands the counterfeit had slipped into?

Lan Sizhui, crouching by the hearth and fanning the embers, broke his train of thought: "Senior Mo, I think the congee is ready."

Wei Wuxian snapped back to the present. He set the wooden spoon down, scooped a mouthful into a clean bowl Sizhui had washed, and took a sip. "It's done. Dish it out and take it to the hall—one bowl each for the poisoned ones. Make sure they finish every drop."

Yet the moment the bowls reached the main hall, a mouthful was all it took for Lan Jingyi to choke, spitting it right back out. "What the hell is this?! Are you trying to poison us?!"

Wei Wuxian clicked his tongue. "Poison? That's your cure! Glutinous rice congee!"

"Setting aside why congee would cure corpse poisoning," Jingyi wheezed, his eyes watering, "I have never tasted congee this spicy in my entire life!"

The other boys who had swallowed a spoonful nodded frantically, tears welling in their eyes. Wei Wuxian rubbed his chin sheepishly. He had grown up in Yunmeng, where the locals were famous for their high spice tolerance, and Wei Wuxian's personal tastes were notoriously extreme. Whenever he cooked, the food turned out spicy enough to make Jiang Cheng slam his bowl down in a cursing fit. But he could never break the habit of tossing in spoonful after spoonful of chili paste; clearly, his hand had slipped again. Curious, Lan Sizhui dipped his spoon into the bowl and took a cautious sip. His face flushed bright crimson in seconds, his lips pressed tight as he forced himself not to spit it out, his eyes turning watery. This flavor... he thought, bewildered, is terrifyingly familiar...

Wei Wuxian cleared his throat. "All medicine tastes a little bitter. A little spice will make you sweat it out—you'll purge the toxin much faster."

A chorus of dubious groans rose from the boys, but they sucked it up and choked the congee down anyway. Within moments, the hall was full of flushed, sweating faces, looking thoroughly miserable. Wei Wuxian shook his head. "Is it really that bad? Hanguang-jun is from Gusu too, and he eats plenty of spice. Why are you all being such babies?"

Sizhui, coughing into his sleeve, stammered, "That's... that's not true, Senior. Hanguang-jun prefers very bland flavors. He never touches spicy food..."

Wei Wuxian froze. "Is that so?"

Yet he remembered clearly that after defecting from the Jiang Clan in his past life, he had crossed paths with Lan Wangji in Yiling. Back then, though his reputation was stained, he hadn't yet become public enemy number one, so he had shamelessly dragged Lan Wangji into a tavern to share a meal and catch up. Lan Wangji had ordered dishes packed to the brim with Sichuan peppercorns and chilies, leading Wei Wuxian to assume their palates were aligned.

Thinking back, he couldn't actually recall if Lan Wangji had lifted his chopsticks once during that meal. Then again, considering he had forgotten his own promise to treat and left Lan Wangji to foot the bill, overlooking such details was hardly surprising.

"Senior... Senior Mo!"

"Hm?" Wei Wuxian blinked, pulling himself out of the memory.

Sizhui kept his voice to a whisper. "The old woman's door... it's open."

A draft crept through the hall, nudging the door to the side chamber ajar, letting it swing lazily back and forth on its hinges. The room was shrouded in murk, but they could make out a hunched silhouette sitting by the table. Wei Wuxian signaled the boys to hold their ground, then slipped quietly inside.

The dim light from the oil lamps outside spilled across the threshold. The old woman kept her chin dipped, seemingly oblivious to his presence. Stretched across her knees was an embroidery hoop with a square of fabric, looking for all the world like a matron occupied with needlework. Her hands, stiff and wooden, were pressed together as she repeatedly attempted to thread a thin strand of string through the eye of a needle.

Wei Wuxian pulled up a stool beside the table. "Why try threading a needle in the dark, Granny? Here, let me."

Taking the needle and thread, he slipped the strand through the eye in a single, fluid motion and handed it back. He rose without a word, stepped out of the room, and pulled the door shut behind him. "Nobody goes in there."

Jin Ling pressed him immediately: "Did you get a good look at her? Is that old hag dead or alive?"

"Mind your manners," Wei Wuxian scolded lightly. "Stop calling her an old hag. That woman is a living corpse."

The boys exchanged uneasy glances. Lan Sizhui asked, "What is a living corpse?"

"A creature that carries every physical hallmark of a corpse, yet remains technically alive," Wei Wuxian explained.

Jin Ling looked stunned. "You're saying she's still a living person?!"

"Did any of you look inside just now?" Wei Wuxian asked.

"We did," they replied.

"What was she doing?"

"Threading a needle."

"Did she manage to get the thread through?"

"...No."

"Exactly. She couldn't. When a body dies, muscle tissue stiffens; it loses the fine motor control required for delicate tasks like threading a needle. Those spots on her face aren't age spots—they're livor mortis. She doesn't eat, yet she still draws breath. She is alive."

Sizhui hesitated. "B-but she is quite elderly. Many old women suffer from poor eyesight and struggle with needles."

"Which is why I threaded it for her," Wei Wuxian replied. "But did any of you catch the other detail? From the second she cracked the front door until now, she hasn't blinked once."

Several disciples blinked reflexively. Wei Wuxian continued, "Living eyes blink to stay lubricated. A corpse has no need for tears. And when I took the needle from her hands, did anyone notice how she looked at me?"

Jin Ling's eyes widened. "Her eyes didn't track you... She turned her whole head!"

"Precisely," Wei Wuxian nodded. "When an ordinary person glances sideways, their pupils naturally shift first. A corpse can't manage that kind of subtle movement; they have to turn their entire skull."

Lan Jingyi scratched his head, looking dazed. "Should we... be taking notes on this?"

Wei Wuxian chuckled. "Good habit. Though out on a night-hunt, you won't have time to flip through a notebook—commit it to memory."

Jin Ling gritted his teeth. "Walking corpses are bad enough. Where the hell did living corpses come from?!"

"Living corpses rarely occur naturally," Wei Wuxian said. "More often than not, they are manufactured. Just like this one."

"Manufactured?! Why on earth would anyone make something like that?!"

"Corpses have obvious drawbacks," Wei Wuxian explained. "Stiff joints, clumsy footing, sluggish movement. But they also have tremendous advantages: they don't feel pain, they can't think for themselves, and they are exceptionally easy to manipulate. Someone clearly thought they could iron out the flaws and engineer a flawless puppet. That was how living corpses were born."

None of the disciples said it out loud, but the collective look on their faces screamed a single name: WEI. WU. XIAN.

Wei Wuxian didn't know whether to laugh or cry. I never invented something this grotesque! he thought defensively, even as a quiet voice admitted that it certainly sounded right up his alley.

Clearing his throat, he said, "Alright, look: Wei Wuxian might have pioneered the general concept, but his experiments produced Wen Ning—the Ghost General. Speaking of which, who came up with that stupid moniker anyway? It sounds ridiculous. Later on, other cultivators tried to copy his work, but lacking the skill to pull it off through proper methods, they took a shortcut and started experimenting on living mortals, resulting in these living corpses." He summed it up: "A botched imitation."

At the mention of Wei Wuxian, Jin Ling's expression hardened into a scowl. "Wei Ying was nothing more than a crooked heretic himself."

Wei Wuxian shrugged. "Sure. Which makes the people manufacturing living corpses the bottom-feeders among heretics."

Lan Sizhui asked, "Senior Mo, what should we do now?"

"Some living corpses don't even realize they've passed on," Wei Wuxian said. "That old woman seems completely detached from reality, so as long as we leave her alone, she won't bother us."

Right then, a sharp, metallic tapping sound rattled through the silence.

It came from directly against one of the windows—a frame boarded shut with heavy black planks. The disciples went deathly pale. Having been relentlessly stalked by that sound ever since stepping foot into Yi City, the mere cadence was enough to make their skin crawl. Wei Wuxian raised a finger to his lips, signaling absolute silence. Holding their breath, the boys watched as he crept toward the boarded window, pressing his eye against a hairline crack between the timber.

The moment he drew near the seam, his vision filled with a wall of pure white. He assumed it was just the thick fog swirling outside—until the white shape abruptly lurched backward.

Staring straight through the crack was a pair of dead, milky-white pupils, glaring into the seam with venomous ferocity. What he had been looking at wasn't the mist at all, but a pair of unblinking, pupilless eyes.
